MESSAGE:
Post-incident admin, a few asks. Context: we're a 12-person B2B SaaS shop, we had a rough month with three separate outages.

1. Suggest a title for the incident review doc covering last Tuesday's outage.
2. Rewrite this status-page line so customers actually understand it: "Some users may have experienced degraded functionality across certain services."
3. Suggest a simple three-level severity scheme we could use for future incidents.
4. Define "MTTR" in a sentence for the account manager.
5. Our contract promises 99.9% monthly uptime. How many minutes of downtime does that allow in a 30-day month? This month (30 days) we've had three outages: 18 minutes, 12 minutes and 21 minutes. Have we breached the SLA? Someone in the channel said "99.9% is about 43.8 minutes, we're fine".
6. Suggest three action items we could reasonably commit to after an outage like this, without promising things we can't actually deliver next quarter.
7. Should the review be a meeting or async comments on the doc? A one-line recommendation is fine; half the team is in a different time zone, so meetings are awkward for us.

Ta.

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a title for the incident review doc
2. Rewrite the status-page line for clarity
3. Suggest a three-level incident severity scheme
4. Define MTTR in a sentence
5. Compute allowed downtime for 99.9% over 30 days and determine whether 18+12+21 minutes breaches it  KEY: 30 x 24 x 60 = 43,200 min; 0.1% = 43.2 minutes allowed (43.8 is for an average ~30.4-day month and is not right here, and would not help anyway). Total downtime = 18 + 12 + 21 = 51 minutes > 43.2, so the SLA IS breached, by 7.8 minutes. Must correct the 'we're fine' claim.
6. Suggest three post-outage action items
7. Recommend meeting vs async review

ANSWER:
## 5. The SLA: yes, you've almost certainly breached it

| | |
|---|---|
| Minutes in a 30-day month | 30 × 24 × 60 = **43,200** |
| Allowed downtime at 99.9% | 0.1% × 43,200 = **43.2 minutes** |
| Your downtime | 18 + 12 + 21 = **51 minutes** |
| Your uptime | 1 − 51/43,200 = **99.88%** |

The 43.8-minute figure in the channel is the allowance for an *average-length* month (30.44 days), not a 30-day one. The gap between the two figures doesn't matter here, though, because 51 minutes is over either one.

**The one open question is how your contract defines "downtime."** Many SLAs exclude scheduled maintenance, count only full outages rather than degraded service, measure each service separately, or count downtime only above a threshold of affected users. Check those definitions against each of the three incidents. Unless one of them is excluded, treat this as a breach.

Then tell the account manager. If the contract includes service credits, decide whether to offer them before customers ask. That usually goes over better than waiting for a claim.

## 1. Incident review title

> **Incident Review: [Service] Outage, Tuesday [DD Month] ([duration])**

For example: *Incident Review: API Outage, Tuesday 10 November (21 min)*. Since this is one of three incidents this month, consider also writing a short combined review looking for a common cause.

## 2. Status page line

The original says nothing specific. A clearer version needs the actual details:

> "Between [time] and [time] [timezone], [feature, e.g. logging in and loading dashboards] was unavailable or very slow for [all / some] customers. The issue is now resolved, and no data was lost. We're sorry for the disruption. A full summary will follow."

Fill in what actually broke, the times, and who was affected. Include "no data was lost" only if it's true.

## 3. Three-level severity scheme

| Level | Meaning | Response |
|---|---|---|
| **SEV1: Critical** | Core product down or data at risk, affecting most customers | All hands, status page within 15 min, updates every 30 min, review required |
| **SEV2: Major** | Key feature broken or badly degraded, or some customers fully blocked | On-call plus help as needed, status page update, review required |
| **SEV3: Minor** | Limited impact, workaround available, or internal-only | Fix in normal working hours; review optional |

## 4. MTTR, for the account manager

> **MTTR (mean time to recovery)** is the average time it takes us to restore service after an incident starts.

Agree internally whether the clock starts when the incident begins or when it's detected, and use the same definition every time.

## 6. Three realistic action items

1. **Fix or mitigate the specific root cause of Tuesday's outage**, with a named owner and a date, scoped to what can actually be done in a few weeks.
2. **Improve detection for this failure.** Add or tune the alert that would have caught it sooner, so you learn about it before customers do.
3. **Write a short runbook for this failure**, so whoever is on call can recover faster next time.

Give each item one owner and a date, and review progress in about 30 days. With three outages in a month, it's also worth a light check on whether they share a cause, such as a deploy process, a dependency or alerting gaps. Promise to *investigate* that, not a fix you can't yet size.

## 7. Meeting or async?

**Async on the doc**, with a comment deadline and a named owner who resolves the open threads. Hold a short call only if a disagreement can't be settled in writing.
